editorNote: A week on the home-computer beat: flying the mail, making words move and watching the software shelf.
morningLine: Home pilots take the mail route; Macintosh owners wait for Jazz.

lead.headline: Solo Flight puts a mail route inside a home-computer cockpit
lead.dek: Best sourced gaming feature; a March review, not a newly verified release.
body: A mail route gives the home pilot a reason to take off. MicroProse’s Solo Flight, reviewed in this month’s COMPUTE!, puts navigation, weather and delivery decisions inside a light-airplane simulation. Sid Meier’s program is listed for the Commodore 64 and Atari computers with at least 48K, a disk drive and joystick, at a publisher price of $34.95.

The screen joins a three-dimensional outside view to an instrument panel. Takeoffs and landings are only the beginning: the pilot must navigate, fly on instruments and cope with emergency procedures. Cursor-key views let the player look left, right and behind the cabin.

Mail Pilot turns the flight into a working journey. Destinations need planning, and every load creates a trade-off between fuel and mail. Navigation accuracy, elapsed time, landing performance and mail delivered all enter the score; worsening weather and higher difficulty make the route less forgiving.

For home-computer owners, the attraction is a game that asks for judgment as well as reflexes. The March review establishes contemporary availability, not a new release this week. The cockpit is already a place to work, explore and play.

stories.headline: After IBM’s PCjr retreat, home-computer owners weigh compatibility and support
stories.dek: Recommended lead: the month’s consequential home-computing business story; explicitly a follow-up, not a new March 25 announcement.
body: IBM’s announced retreat from the PCjr leaves owners with practical questions about software and expansion. The March 19 announcement calls for production to end in April; it is not a notice that support has already ceased.

March COMPUTE! describes snap-on 128K expansion modules that can bring the machine to 512K, together with a replacement typewriter-style keyboard. Yet memory size alone does not make this home computer interchangeable with an IBM PC.

Charles Brannon identifies memory-layout and DOS 2.1 configuration problems. In some configurations, even a 512K PCjr cannot run a program designed for a 128K PCjr. Buyers weighing remaining stock have more to investigate than the number on a memory label.

stories.headline: A $12.95 disk challenges the commercial word processor
stories.dek: Practical consumer-software story with verified pricing.
body: A magazine listing is making an unusually direct challenge to the word-processing shelf. Charles Brannon’s SpeedScript 3.0 appears in March COMPUTE!, with an optional Commodore 64 disk priced at $12.95 plus $2 shipping and handling in the United States and Canada.

The machine-language program occupies approximately 6K. Insertion, deletion, screen editing, margins, centering, headers and footers turn it into a practical writing tool. Readers may enter the published listing through MLX instead of ordering the disk.

The update draws on roughly a year of enhancements, suggestions and debugging. VIC-20, Atari and Apple II versions are promised for future issues; they are not supplied by this installment. The magazine calls the companion disk an experiment, not a public-domain distribution.

stories.headline: Jazz misses its late-March date as Macintosh waits for office software
stories.dek: Owner-focused follow-up to a March 19 announcement, documented in a fully retrieved contemporary newspaper report. Not a new announcement this week.
body: The Macintosh office-software shelf must wait longer for Lotus Jazz. Kathleen Day’s March 20 report says Lotus moved its expected late-March shipment to May 27 after notifying authorized dealers.

Lotus and Apple describe the problems as minor, but the delay matters to an installed base awaiting integrated office software. May 27 remains a projected shipment date, not evidence that copies have shipped.

Apple chief John Sculley’s estimate that half of Macintosh purchasers would buy Jazz is a forecast, not measured adoption. Dealers and owners face the simpler question of when a finished product will reach the counter.

worldAnchor.headline: Geneva negotiators begin detailed medium-range nuclear talks
worldAnchor.summary: U.S. and Soviet negotiators held their first detailed medium-range nuclear-arms session in Geneva on March 28. A secrecy agreement kept negotiating details private as the resumed arms talks continued.

bbsNote.headline: The race to 2400 bps meets a chip bottleneck
bbsNote.summary: Arlon R. Levitan, Telecomputing Today: The Race To Talk Fast, COMPUTE! March 1985, pp.87–88. Period analysis and reported forecasts, not independently confirmed delivery schedules.

posts.text: Hayes, Novation, U.S. Robotics, Racal-Vadic and other firms announced 2400-bps units at the preceding November COMDEX. Levitan reports $800–$900 pricing and warns of QAM-chip constraints; projected availability is a columnist’s forecast. 2400 bps is eight times 300 bps and twice 1200 bps.
The column identifies the Health Forum as a new special-interest group, moderated by sysop Bob Walter, for fitness-related discussions.
Billiam Coronel’s computer humor appears in the User Publishing Area; the column notes that back issues are available.

The column reports a dispute over promotional messages. People/Link interpreted removal language as deletion of its email; CompuServe denied deleting email and said it enforced its policy against commercial SIG messages. Do not repeat the Chicago free-access promotion as current: it was scheduled to end March 1.

curiosity.detail: The Model 305 costs $99.95 and is advertised as turning a color composite monitor into a TV with a switch. This is a period ad, not a verified launch date or a claim that the price includes a display.
